titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §112–126: carriage, debt-hostages and deposits (xviii 50 – xxi 24)
part: Laws §112–126 · carriage, debt-hostages & deposits (Col. xviii 50 – xxi 24)
about: Fifteen laws on goods entrusted to other people. The first are the carriage laws: a man away on a journey gives silver, gold and goods to a man to carry, and if the carrier keeps what he was meant to deliver he is convicted and pays five times its value (§112). Then the debt-hostage laws: a creditor who helps himself to grain from a debtor’s bin or storehouse, without the owner’s say, loses his whole loan and returns what he took (§113); one who holds no debt yet seizes a person pays a third of a mina for each (§114); a hostage who dies a natural death in the creditor’s house costs him nothing (§115), but one who dies from beating or neglect costs the creditor his own son, if the hostage was a free man’s son, or a third of a mina and his loan, if a slave (§116). Debt can also put a man’s wife, son and daughter into service for three years, with release in the fourth (§117); a slave handed over can be sold on by the merchant (§118), but the slave-woman who has borne her master children can be redeemed (§119). The last six laws are on deposits: grain stored in another man’s house, lost or taken or denied there, is doubled by the one who took or denied it (§120), and storing grain costs five qa per kor a year (§121); valuables given for safekeeping need witnesses and a contract, and without them there is no claim (§122–123), while a depositary who denies a deposit made before witnesses pays double (§124); a house-owner in whose house a deposit is lost, through a breach or a crossing-over that also took his own goods, must make good what he was careless with and then look to the thief himself (§125); and a false report of loss turns the claim round on the one who made it (§126). Harper’s transliteration is followed with his glossary; where a Sumerogram stands on the plate behind a printed Akkadian word (Á for hire, KI.UD for the storehouse, the fraction one third, the capacity sign SÌLA) the note says how far the identification can be checked, and two readings, ubâršuma and babtašu in §126, are given with their alternative.

sentences.l: If a-man on-the-road is-staying-and, silver gold stone and the-goods of-his-hand to a-man he-gave-and, for-transport he-made-carry-him,
sentences.i: If a man is away on a journey and has given silver, gold, stones and his own goods to a man, and had him carry them as a consignment,
sentences.n: The carriage laws begin; this first law is a long “if”. ina ḫarrānim wašib “he is staying on the road” (wašābum, to dwell, stay): the owner is away. Three goods stand side by side, kaspam ḫurāṣam abnam, then u bīš qātīšu: bīšum is Harper’s “property, possessions”, here in the short construct form bīš, and qātīšu is “of his hands” (so spelled in the earlier parts), so “his own goods”. abnum is simply “stone”; beside silver and gold it presumably means precious stones. iddinma is nadānum, “to give”, with -ma “and”. A šubultum (Harper: “goods for transportation”) is a consignment; ušābilšu is the Š-stem of wabālum “to carry”, so “he had (him) carry”. Uncertain: whether -šu is “him” (the carrier) or “it” (the consignment).

sentences.l: that man, whatever that was-sent, where it-was-sent not he-gave-and, he-took-away,
sentences.i: that man did not give what was sent to the place where it was sent, but took it away,
sentences.n: awīlum šū, “that man”, takes the carrier up again; the first man is out of the picture. mimma ša šūbulu is “whatever (was) sent”, ašar šūbulu “where (it) was sent”: ša and ašar both take the subjunctive -u on the verb. Harper reads šu-bu-lu as the Š-stem of wabālum; read here as the Š stative šūbul (long ū) with the subjunctive -u, “has been sent” (UNCERTAIN: the exact force of the Š stative; the sense “was sent” is clear). lā iddinma is “he did not give”; lā is the negative inside an “if” clause. itbal is tabālum, Harper’s “to take away, take possession of”, in the preterite (the perfect would be ittabal).

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-consignment, that man, in whatever that was-sent-and not he-gave, they-shall-convict-him-and,
sentences.i: the owner of the consignment — they shall convict that man of everything that was sent and that he did not give —
sentences.n: bēl šibultim, “the owner of the consignment”, is the claimant. ukannūšuma is kânum in the D-stem, “to convict, prove against” (uktīn, ukannūšuma): this is the D present with the plural ending -ū, which makes it an impersonal “they shall convict him”, the court or the witnesses, which is why the owner is set at the head of the sentence and not made its subject; -šu is “him” and -ma carries the sentence on. The charge is ina mimma ša šūbulūma lā iddinu, “regarding whatever was sent and which he did not give”: two verbs under one ša, each with the subjunctive -u (šūbulu + -ma gives šūbulūma).

sentences.l: that man up-to five-fold whatever that was-given-to-him to the-owner of-the-consignment he-shall-give.
sentences.i: and that man shall give the owner of the consignment five times whatever was given to him.
sentences.n: The penalty is a multiple of the loss: a-du 5-šu, “up to its fivefold” (the plate shows the sign DU, so Harper’s a-du is said adu, a variant of adi). The 5 is the numeral, five wedges, with -šu “its”. innadnušum is the N-stem passive (preterite) of nadānum with the dative -šum: “(which) was given to him”; the subjunctive -u comes before the dative suffix. The last verb is inaddin, “he shall give”, the present used for the code’s “shall”.

sentences.l: If a-man upon a-man grain and silver he-has-and, without the-owner of-grain, from-the-bin or from-the-storehouse, grain he-took,
sentences.i: If a man has a claim of grain and silver on a man, and without the consent of the owner of the grain has taken grain from the bin or from the storehouse,
sentences.n: A creditor’s self-help. eli awīlim … išûma, “he has (grain and silver) upon a man”, makes him the creditor; išû, “to have”, with -ma “and”. ina balum bēl šeʾim is “without the owner of the grain” (the English “without the consent of” is idiom; the words say “without the owner of the grain”); ina našpakim, “from the bin” (našpakum, Harper’s “heap, bin”) and ina maškanim, “from the storehouse” (maškanum, Harper’s “granary, storage-house”), the two places the grain was kept. ulu (written u₂-lu) is “or”. ilteqi is the perfect of leqûm, “to take”, with KI read qi: “he took”. The grain is written with the one sign ŠE, no ending; the case comes from the grammar. Whose store it was is not said.

sentences.l: that man, without the-owner of-grain, from-the-bin or from-the-storehouse, for-the-taking of-grain they-shall-convict-him-and, the-grain as-much-as he-took he-shall-return,
sentences.i: they shall convict that man of taking grain from the bin or the storehouse without the owner’s consent, and he shall return the grain, as much as he took,
sentences.n: The verdict repeats the charge word for word. ina šeʾim leqîm, “for the taking of grain”: leqîm (li-qi₂-im) is the infinitive of leqûm with its genitive ending, after ina. In line 9 the storehouse is not spelled out as in the first law but written with a Sumerogram, which Harper’s glossary names KISLAḪ for maškanum. On the plate (Plate 29, XIX 9) it is two signs, KI and UD, and that is how it is written here; Harper’s List of Signs has no entry for the pair, and the single sign KISAL (his no. 103) is a different shape. ukannūšuma as in §112. mala ilqû, “as much as he took” (subjunctive -u), and utâr is the D-stem of târum, “to give back”, in the present.

sentences.l: and from whatever its-name, as-much-as he-gave, he-forfeits.
sentences.i: and he shall forfeit whatever it is, as much as he gave.
sentences.n: The second penalty, and the sting: ina mimma šumšu, “from anything whatever its name” (šumum), mala iddinu “as much as he gave”: the creditor loses the whole of his loan. ītelli (written i-te-el-li) is elûm, “to go up”, used for “to forfeit”, the house spelling; the same word as in §35 and §37.

sentences.l: If a-man upon a-man grain and silver not he-has-and, his-hostage he-has-distrained,
sentences.i: If a man has no claim of grain or silver on a man, and has distrained a hostage of his,
sentences.n: The same opening as §113, now with lā īšuma, “he does not have”: this creditor has no debt owing, and still seizes a person. nibūtum is Harper’s “hostage for debt” (from nebûm, “to distrain, seize as pledge”); here ni-bu-zu, nibūssu, “his hostage”, with the sign ZU doing duty for -ssu (nibūt + šu). ittebi is the perfect of nebûm, “he has distrained”. (Harper reads b throughout; later dictionaries write the same words with p, nepûm and nipûtum, since the signs BI and BU also read pi and pu; the signs are the same either way.) Whose hostage it is — a person of the other man’s household — is read from the sense.

sentences.l: for-a-hostage one, a-third a-mina of-silver he-shall-weigh-out.
sentences.i: he shall weigh out one-third of a mina of silver for each hostage.
sentences.n: ana nibūtim ištiat is “for hostage, one”: for each person taken. ⅓ MA.NA kaspim, “a third of a mina of silver”, is twenty shekels, since the mina is sixty. The fraction is a single sign on the plate, two uprights over a long horizontal; Harper’s list of numerals draws one third as a longer group, so the character used here is only the nearest Unicode sign, and the identification is uncertain; the spoken form šalšāt is reconstructed (marked (?) in the glossary). išaqqal is šaqālum, “to weigh out”, i.e. to pay.

sentences.l: If a-man upon a-man grain and silver he-has-and, his-hostage he-distrained-and,
sentences.i: If a man has a claim of grain and silver on a man, and has distrained his hostage,
sentences.n: The law of §114 turned round: the creditor does have a claim, and takes a hostage. ibbi is another form of nebûm (Harper lists ib-bi under the same verb, the plain preterite), joined to the next clause by -ma.

sentences.l: the-hostage in the-house of-her-distrainer in-her-fates she-died, that case a-claim not it-has.
sentences.i: and the hostage dies a natural death in the distrainer’s house, that case has no claim.
sentences.n: bīt nēbīša is “the house of her distrainer” (bīt, the construct state, written É). nēbīša is the one who holds her (nebûm again, as a noun: the -ša is the hostage’s, a grammatical feminine; the noun’s exact shape is UNCERTAIN). ina šīmātīša imtūt, “in her fates she died”: šīmtum, fate, in the plural, as ana šīmtim alākum “to go to one’s fate” in §12 means to die; a death by fate is a natural death, set against the beating and neglect of §116. imtūt is mâtum, “to die”, perfect. dīnum šū rugummâm ul īšu, “that case has no claim”: rugummûm is the claim a lawsuit can bring, and the sentence closes the matter, with ul and īšu in the house spelling of išûm.

sentences.l: If the-hostage in the-house of-her-distrainer through-beating or through-neglect she-died,
sentences.i: If the hostage dies in the distrainer’s house from beating or from neglect,
sentences.n: The same case, but the death is not natural. maḫāṣum is Harper’s “beating, abuse, injury” (a noun from maḫāṣum, to strike), written ma-ḫa-ṣi-im, the ṣi being the sign ZI; uššušum is his “neglect”, written uš-šu-ši-im. Both stand after ina, “through”, and ulu is “or”. The verb is the imtūt of §115.

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-hostage his-merchant shall-convict-and,
sentences.i: the owner of the hostage shall convict his merchant,
sentences.n: tamkāršu, “his merchant”, is the creditor who took the hostage (written DAM.GÀR + šu). ukānma is the singular present of the verb of §112, kânum in the D-stem, “he shall convict”, with -ma carrying the sentence on to the penalty.

sentences.l: if a-son of-a-man, his-son they-shall-kill;
sentences.i: if it was a man’s son, they shall kill his son;
sentences.n: A life for a life: mār awīlim, “the son of a man”, is the hostage; māršu, “his son”, is the merchant’s, by the sense, though the sentence does not say whose. idukkū is dâkum, “to kill”, in the plural active, “they shall kill” (compare idukkūšuma in §21), not the passive iddâk of the other death sentences.

sentences.l: if a-slave of-a-man, a-third a-mina of-silver he-shall-weigh-out, and from whatever its-name, as-much-as he-gave, he-forfeits.
sentences.i: if a man’s slave, he shall weigh out one-third of a mina of silver, and he shall forfeit whatever it is, as much as he gave.
sentences.n: If the hostage was a man’s slave (warad awīlim, ARAD, with no ending written), the merchant pays a third of a mina, as in §114, and loses his loan as in §113. The wording is the formula already met; only the first words are new.

sentences.l: If a-debt has-seized-him-and, his-wife, his-son and his-daughter for silver he-gave, or for-service he-has-handed-over,
sentences.i: If a debt has seized a man and he has given his wife, his son and his daughter for silver, or has handed them over into service,
sentences.n: A debt-slavery law. šumma awīlam, with awīlam in the accusative, because the debt (eḫiltum, Harper’s “debt”) is the subject and the man its object: iṣbassuma, “it seized him, and” (ṣabātum, preterite iṣbat + -šu + -ma, with ZU for -ssu). The three persons are written with Sumerograms: SAL-zu, “his wife”; DUMU-šu, “his son”; DUMU.SAL-zu, “his daughter”. The last is DUMU + SAL + ZU on the plate (three signs after ù); Harper prints mâra-zu for it. ana kaspim iddin is “he gave for silver”, ulu ana kiššātim ittandin “or he handed them over into service” (kiššātum, Harper’s kiššatu “service”, a different word from the kiššatum “totality” of the prologue); ittandin is the perfect of nadānum with the extra -n- Harper’s transliteration shows.

sentences.l: three years the-house of-their-buyer and of-their-master they-shall-work; in-the-fourth year their-release it-shall-be-set.
sentences.i: they shall work three years in the house of their buyer and their master, and in the fourth year their release shall be set.
sentences.n: MU 3{kam} is “year, three” and is said šalāš šanātim, “three years” (the spoken form is reconstructed, as in §42–§51; at §30 the same signs mean “the third year”). bīt šāyamānišunu u kāšišišunu, “the house of their buyer and of their master” (bīt is the construct state; šayyāmānum, kāšišum; Harper glossary: purchaser, master), with ippešū, “they shall do (work)”, from epēšum, written i-ib-bi-šu: the house is not preceded by ina, so it is a place accusative, “in the house”. ina rebûtim šattim is “in the fourth year”. andurārum is Harper’s “freedom” (written an-du-ra-ar), the release from debt-service; andurāršunu iššakkan, “their release shall be set (put)” — the N-stem present of šakānum, as in §105.

sentences.l: If a-male-slave or a-female-slave for service he-has-handed-over,
sentences.i: If a man has handed a male or a female slave over into service,
sentences.n: The same debt-service, now with slaves: wardam (ARAD) and amtam (GEME₂, the signs SAL and KUR), each with the accusative -am. kiššātim, “into service”, is spelled ki-iš-ša-tim here and ki-iš-ša-a-tim in §117; the subject, the owner, is not named. ittandin as in §117.

sentences.l: the-merchant has-passed-on; for silver he-gives; not he-shall-be-claimed.
sentences.i: and the merchant passes the slave on and sells the slave for silver, no claim shall be made on the slave.
sentences.n: Here the merchant who holds the slave is free to move him on. ušētiq is etēqum, “to pass”, in the Š-stem (causative), preterite: “he made (him) pass (to another)”; ana kaspim inaddin, “for silver he gives”, is sale. ul ibbaqqar is the N-stem of baqārum (Harper’s BAKARU IV), “he shall not be claimed”: nobody can reclaim the slave from the buyer. Uncertain: whether ušētiq belongs to the merchant’s act of passing on or to the owner’s. Because ušētiq is a preterite, not a permission, the two verbs are read as a further condition (the English present, “passes on and sells”, covers both), with the ruling in ul ibbaqqar; either way the sense is that the merchant may sell him on and the buyer cannot be claimed against.

sentences.l: If a-debt has-seized-him-and, his-slave-woman who sons she-bore-him, for silver he-has-given,
sentences.i: If a debt has seized a man and he has sold his slave-woman, who has borne him sons, for silver,
sentences.n: The same debt, now with a slave-woman who has borne her master children. amassu is GEME₂-zu, “his slave-woman”; ša mārī ulidūšum, “who sons bore to him” (walādum, preterite ūlid with the subjunctive -u and the dative -šum; Harper’s spelling ul-du-šum is shortened, so the vowels are UNCERTAIN). “Sons” is DUMU with the plural marker {meš} (the signs ME and ESH), Harper’s mârê: a plural of mārum, which may include daughters, so “children” is as possible as “sons”. it-ta-din is the perfect of nadānum, “he has given”: here sold.

sentences.l: the-silver that-the-merchant weighed-out, the-owner of-the-slave-woman he-shall-weigh-out-and, his-slave-woman he-shall-redeem.
sentences.i: the owner of the slave-woman shall weigh out the silver the merchant paid, and redeem his slave-woman.
sentences.n: The mother of children is not lost for good: kaspam tamkārum išqulu, “the silver (that) the merchant weighed out” (a ša-less relative clause with the subjunctive -u), is repaid by bēl amtim, “the owner of the slave-woman”, and then amassu ipaddar, “he shall redeem his slave-woman” (padārum, Harper’s “to ransom”). The man who sold her may buy her back; the buyer may not keep her.

sentences.l: If a-man his-grain for-storage in-the-house of-a-man he-has-heaped-and, in-the-granary an-accident has-occurred,
sentences.i: If a man has stored his grain for storage in a man’s house, and an accident has happened in the granary,
sentences.n: The first of the deposit laws, on grain. ŠE-šu is “his grain”, šeʾišu. ana našpakūtim is “for storage” (the abstract in -ūtum, “being stored”, built on našpakum, Harper’s “heap, bin”; compare maṣṣarūtum “safekeeping”). The text has bīt awīlum, with -lum, where the genitive -lim is expected: Harper prints a-wi-lum as it stands. išpukma is šapākum, “to heap up, store”, with -ma. garītum is Harper’s “store-house, granary”. ibbûm (i-ib-bu-u-um) is his “accident”; the grain is damaged or lost by something outside anyone’s fault, and what follows says who bears it. ittabši is the perfect of the N-stem of bašûm, “to be there, come about”: “has happened”. Uncertain: ibbûm and its sense of “accident”, as it occurs only here.

sentences.l: or the-owner of-the-house the-bin he-has-opened-and grain he-took, or the-grain that in-his-house was-stored for-the-whole he-denied,
sentences.i: or the owner of the house has opened the bin and taken grain, or has denied altogether the grain that was stored in his house,
sentences.n: Two more things that can go wrong, both the house-owner’s doing. iptēma is petûm, “to open”, in the perfect, and ilqi “he took” as in §113. The second charge is a ša-clause: šeʾam ša ina bītišu iššapku, “the grain that in his house was stored”, with iššapku the N-stem (passive) of šapākum and its subjunctive -u. ana gamrim ittakir, “for the whole (ana gamrim) he denied”: gamrum is Harper’s “complete, total”, so the owner denies the whole deposit; ittakir is nakārum, “to deny, disown”, as in §106. bītišu is written É-ti-šu: the sign É, a phonetic -ti and -šu. našpakam is spelled na-aš-pa-kam, the last syllable written with the sign KAM (on the plate a diamond with a hook inside, not the GA sign of ga-ri-tim in §120).

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-grain before the-god his-grain shall-prove-and, the-owner of-the-house the-grain that he-took shall-double-and to the-owner of-the-grain shall-give.
sentences.i: the owner of the grain shall prove his grain before the god, and the owner of the house shall double the grain he took and give it to the owner of the grain.
sentences.n: The ruling. maḫar ilim, “before the god”: the proof is made in front of the deity, the same phrase as in §9. ubârma is bârum in the D-stem, “to prove, establish” (Harper: “to declare, itemize”): the owner states and proves the amount of his grain. Then the house-owner pays double: šeʾam ša ilqû, “the grain that he took”, uštašannâma, “he shall double (it), and” — the Š-stem perfect of §101, still not secure in its stem, read “double” from the sense of the penalty — and ana bēl šeʾim inaddin, “to the owner of the grain he shall give”.

sentences.l: If a-man in-the-house of-a-man grain he-has-heaped, per-year for one kor five qa of-grain the-hire of-the-bin he-shall-give.
sentences.i: If a man has stored grain in a man’s house, he shall give, each year, five qa of grain for each kor as the hire of the bin.
sentences.n: The price of storage. išpuk is the plain preterite of šapākum (§120 had išpukma). ina šanat, “in the year” (šanat, a form of šattum), means “each year”. The rate: ana 1 ŠE.GUR.E, “for one kor of grain” (the signs ŠE, GUR and a final E; E is as in GAN.E, the bur, in §44), ḫamšat qa šeʾim, “five qa of grain”. The numeral 5 is five wedges (Harper’s V) and the measure is the sign he reads QA, qa, about a litre; the plate draws it as a diamond with a cross, which I take to be SÌLA. Á našpakim is “the hire of the bin”: Harper’s ID is the ideogram for hire, idum (his glossary lists it among the Sumerian ideograms, with -šu and -ša). On the plate it is one sign, A₂ (Á, “arm; hire”), the same sign that spells it in ittabši and not the river sign A.ENGUR, so “hire” rests on his list and not on a spelled word, and the case ending is not written. Five qa for three hundred: a little under two per cent a year.

sentences.l: If a-man to a-man silver, gold and anything its-name for-safekeeping he-gives,
sentences.i: If a man gives silver, gold or anything else to a man for safekeeping,
sentences.n: Deposits of valuables. The present inaddin, “he gives”, stands in the “if” clause, and in this law ana maṣṣarūtim, “for safekeeping” (maṣṣarūtum, “guarding”), is the whole purpose of the gift. u mimma šumšu, “and anything whatever its name”, covers everything else. KÙ.GI is the gold sign, written with no ending.

sentences.l: whatever as-much-as he-gives, witnesses he-shall-show, contracts he-shall-set-and, for-safekeeping he-shall-give.
sentences.i: all that he gives he shall show to witnesses, and he shall set up contracts, and give it for safekeeping.
sentences.n: The formalities, in a row of -ma verbs. mimma mala inaddinu is “whatever, as much as, he gives”, a relative clause with the subjunctive -u. šībī ukallam: ukallam is the D present of kalāmum (Harper: KALAMU, “to show, inform”), “he shall show”, with šībī “witnesses”: the goods are shown to witnesses (the object, the goods, is the clause just before it). riksātim išakkanma, “he shall set (make) contracts”: riksātum is “bond, contract” (Harper), šakānum “to place”. Only then ana maṣṣarūtim inaddin. Without witnesses and contract the depositor has nothing to show: §123.

sentences.l: If without witnesses and contracts for-safekeeping he-gave-and, where he-gave they-denied-him, that case a-claim not it-has.
sentences.i: If he has given it for safekeeping without witnesses and contracts, and they deny him where he gave it, that case has no claim.
sentences.n: The other side of §122: balum šībī u riksātim, “without witnesses and contracts” (balum takes the genitive; the same “without” as in §113). ašar iddinu, “where he gave (it)”, subjunctive -u. ittakrūšu is the plural perfect of nakārum, “they have denied him” (the denial may come from the depositary and his household). The closing sentence is the one of §115: the case has no claim, ul īšu.

sentences.l: If a-man to a-man silver, gold and anything its-name before witnesses for-safekeeping he-gave-and, he-denied-him,
sentences.i: If a man has given silver, gold or anything else to a man for safekeeping before witnesses, and he denies him,
sentences.n: The case with witnesses. maḫar šībī, “before witnesses”, is what §123’s depositor lacked. ittakiršu is the perfect of nakārum, “he has denied”, with -šu “him”: the depositary denies the depositor.

sentences.l: that man they-shall-convict-him-and, whatever that he-denied he-shall-double-and he-shall-give.
sentences.i: they shall convict that man, and he shall give double whatever he denied.
sentences.n: ukannūšuma as in §112. mimma ša ikkiru, “whatever that he denied”, is a relative clause with the subjunctive -u (the same verb as in §107); uštašannâma, as in §120, is “he shall double (it), and”. The penalty is twice the amount denied.

sentences.l: If a-man his-goods for-safekeeping he-gave-and, where he-gave,
sentences.i: If a man has given his goods for safekeeping, and, where he gave them,
sentences.n: The last of the deposit laws and the longest sentence of the part: one “if” in four stages. First the deposit: mimmâšu, “his goods”, ana maṣṣarūtim iddinma. ašar iddinu, “where he gave (it)”, is the place of the deposit, and the sentence goes on to say what happened there.

sentences.l: or by-a-breach or by-a-pillaging his-goods with the-goods of the-owner of-the-house have-been-lost; the-owner of-the-house who was-careless-and,
sentences.i: or through a breach or through a crossing-over (?) his goods have been lost together with the goods of the owner of the house; the owner of the house, who was careless, and
sentences.n: pilšum (Harper prints bi-il-ši-im; the first sign, BI, is read pi₂ here) is a breach, a hole through a wall; nabalkattum is Harper’s “pillage”; the earlier part gap-b takes it as “crossing-over” (from nabalkutum, to cross over), so a way into the house over the wall as against through it (UNCERTAIN); it is written na-ba-al-ka-at-tim, a word the stone splits over two lines (XX 71 ends na-ba-, XX 72 begins al-ka-at-tim). itti mimmê bēl bītim, “with the goods of the owner of the house”: the depositor’s goods were lost along with the house-owner’s own. iḫtaliq is ḫalāqum, “to be lost”, perfect. Line XX 75 is one long stele line carrying two clauses: iḫtaliq closes the loss, and bēl bītim ša igûma begins the verdict, “the owner of the house who was careless” (egûm, “to be negligent”, with -ma).

sentences.l: whatever that for safekeeping they-gave-to-him-and he-caused-to-be-lost, he-shall-make-good-and, to the-owner of-the-property he-shall-restore.
sentences.i: shall make good whatever was given to him for safekeeping and which he caused to be lost, and restore it to the owner of the property.
sentences.n: The verdict, which belongs with the end of the unit before. mimma ša ana maṣṣarūtim iddinūšumma uḫalliqu: ša takes two verbs with the subjunctive -u, “whatever they gave him for safekeeping and (which) he lost” (iddinūšumma, with the dative -šum; uḫalliqu is the D-stem of ḫalāqum, “to make vanish”). ušallamma is šalāmum, D present, “he shall make good” (Harper: “to restore”); iriab is riābum, “to replace”, in the present. makkūrum, “property”, is written with the Sumerogram Harper gives as ŠA-GA, printed with a hyphen here; the plate’s signs are read as in §6.

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-house his-goods lost he-shall-seek-out-and, from his-thief he-shall-take.
sentences.i: The owner of the house shall search out his lost goods and take them from his thief.
sentences.n: The house-owner has paid the depositor; now he looks for his own loss. mimmâšu ḫalqam, “his goods, the lost (goods)”, the object of ištenēʾima, from šeʾûm “to seek”, which Harper lists as “to search for”; the form (iš-te-ne-i-ma) has the infix -ten- of the Gtn stem, the stem of repeated action, in the present: “he shall search about” (the stem analysis is mine, from the form, UNCERTAIN). itti šarrāqānišu ileqqi, “from his thief he shall take”: šarrāqānum is the thief in question, and the house-owner recoups from him, not from the depositor.

sentences.l: If a-man his-goods not lost-and, his-goods lost he-said, his-babtum he-has-accused,
sentences.i: If a man’s goods are not lost, but he says that his goods are lost, and has made a claim against the one he holds liable,
sentences.n: The last law of the part: a false report of loss. lā ḫaliqma, “is not lost, and”, then mimmēšu ḫaliq iqtabi, “his goods (are) lost, he said”: ḫaliq is the stative, iqtabi the perfect of qabûm, “to say”. babtum is Harper’s “loss, defects” (written ba-ab-ta-šu), and utebbir (u-te-ib-bi-ir) his “to file a claim for” (abārum, “to accuse”; Harper’s stem II,2, the reflexive of the D-stem, here a preterite). Harper brackets mi-im-[me]-šu: the oblique-looking mimmēšu where a subject is expected is as he prints it. Uncertain: I take babtašu as the person he holds responsible, “his babtum”, which the rest of the law needs (a payment to him in the last line); on Harper’s reading, “he filed a claim for his loss”, the same sentence would stand with babtašu as the loss, but then ana babtišu in the last line is not a payment to anyone. He also brackets ḫa-li-[iq]. Later dictionaries have babtum as a city quarter or ward, which would make “his babtum” the accused man’s quarter; Harper’s “loss, defects” is the base here, and the person held liable is the nearest to both.

sentences.l: since his-goods not lost, his-babtum before the-god he-shall-prove-him-and,
sentences.i: since his goods were not lost, the one he accused shall prove it against him before the god, and
sentences.n: kīma mimmûšu lā ḫalqu, “since his goods are not lost” (kīma, “since, when”, with the stative ḫalqu and the subjunctive -u). Then babtašu ina maḫar ilim ubâršuma: ubâršu is bârum, D, “he shall prove”, as in §120, with -šu “him”; babtašu is the subject, set first, and -šu is “him”, the claimant: “his babtum, before the god, shall prove him”, i.e. the accused proves the matter against the man who accused him, here that the goods were never lost. Uncertain: who the subject of ubâršuma is. The other reading takes babtašu as the object, taken up by -šu, with the claimant as the subject; Harper’s own gloss for ubâršu is “to declare, to itemize”. “Prove” stays as the base sense of bârum.

sentences.l: whatever that he-claimed he-shall-double-and, to his-babtum he-shall-give.
sentences.i: and he shall give double whatever he claimed to the one he accused.
sentences.n: ša irgumu: ragāmum, “to claim”, with the subjunctive -u: “whatever he claimed (as lost)”. uštašannâma as in §120 and §124, “he shall double (it), and”. ana babtišu inaddin: the false claimant pays the amount, doubled, to the man he accused. If babtum were only the loss and not the party (see the first unit of the law), this last phrase would be “to his loss”, which makes no sense as a payment; that is why it is read as the person. The next law, §127, begins on the following stele line, XXI 25.
